warmup.q: A loader thread runs registry.current = new RateCard("EUR", fees);. The field current is a plain field, and RateCard's own fields are plain too. A request thread reads registry.current and gets a card that isn't null. What can card.currency() return?
options: Always "EUR": the constructor finished before the reference was stored
null, until the loader thread ends
warmup.why: Nothing links the loader's writes to the request thread's reads, so they may become visible in any order. The reader can see the reference before the write of the currency, and then it reads the field's starting value, null. The constructor did run first in the loader (option 1), but that says nothing about what another thread sees. The first section shows it happening in a real run.

opening:
Picture writing a letter to a friend. You write three pages, fold them into an envelope, seal it and give it to a courier. Your friend opens it and reads all three pages. Nobody worries that the courier might deliver the envelope while page three is still on your desk.

Java programs hand objects between threads like this all day. (A thread is one path of work running beside others in the same program.) A loader thread runs registry.current = new RateCard("EUR", fees);. The constructor writes the pages, and the assignment hands over the envelope. Yet another thread can read registry.current, find a real rate card, and see null where its currency should be.

It's an easy trap, because the line reads in one direction: build, then store. In the thread that runs it, that's what happens. The last lesson showed how a volatile field makes one new value visible to other threads, but an object is many fields. In this lesson, we'll watch an object arrive half-written, seal the envelope four ways, see what final fields promise, and keep a constructor from showing its object too early. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a letter that arrived with blank pages, because nothing sealed the envelope. We sealed it four ways, glued the important pages in with final, and kept the house shut until the builders were done.

Now search your own code for constructors that call register(this) or addListener(this), start a thread, or pass this:: to anything. Each one shows an unfinished object to someone. Then look for shared fields that hold objects and are neither final nor volatile.

Next, we'll build an object only when the first thread asks for it, like a shop that opens its stockroom for the first customer, and ask why checking twice needs volatile.

sections.h: Handing over an object is a write, and readers can see it half-built
sections.html:
When a customer pays by card, the card company charges the shop a small fee, say 1.20 euros for a VISA payment. The shop's program keeps these fees in a RateCard: a currency, and a fee for each card brand. A loader thread builds a new rate card whenever the fees change. The request threads, which handle the payments, read the current one.

Handing an object to another thread like this is called publishing it: storing a reference to it where another thread can find it, such as a shared field, a static field or a collection. (A reference is the value a variable holds to point at an object.) Here is the loader's side:

Java
// Naive: publishing through a plain field
RateCard card = new RateCard("EUR", fees);   // 1. make the object, 2. run the constructor
registry.current = card;                     // 3. publish: store the reference where others look
Kotlin
// Naive: publishing through a plain field
val card = RateCard("EUR", fees)             // 1. make the object, 2. run the constructor
registry.current = card                      // 3. publish: store the reference where others look

Three things happen. The JVM, the program that runs your Java code, makes the object with every field at its default value: 0, false or null. The constructor writes the real values. Then the reference is stored in current. In the loader thread, they happen in exactly that order.

A request thread that reads current gets no such promise. A write is guaranteed visible to a read in another thread only when a happens-before edge links them. A write to a volatile field, a field whose reads always see the latest write, and a later read of that field form one such edge. Happens-before, the rules that matter, lists them all. Here, nothing links the request thread's read to the loader's writes. So two layers are free to change the order. The JIT, the compiler inside the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while it runs, may move the store of the reference ahead of the constructor's stores. And the processor may show its stores to its other cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, in a different order. ARM processors, such as the ones in Apple Silicon laptops, do this more than Intel and AMD processors. A request thread can then see current != null and still read a null currency or a fee of 0. That's called a partially constructed object, and no line you wrote creates one.

In the letter's terms, the courier delivered the envelope before all the pages were inside. The figure shows it. The picture breaks in one place: a real courier can't carry pages you haven't written yet. Here the reordering happens in layers you never see, and the code gives no hint of it.

It isn't only theory. jcstress, a tool from OpenJDK (the open-source project that builds Java), runs tiny tests on several threads at once, millions of times, and counts every result. It has a sample called BasicJMM_08_Finals. One thread publishes an object with four plain int fields, set to 1, 2, 3 and 4, through a plain field. Another thread reads the four fields. Here is the run recorded in the sample, on an x86_64 machine (the Intel and AMD kind), where -1 means the reader didn't see the object yet:

          RESULT      SAMPLES     FREQ       EXPECT  DESCRIPTION
  -1, -1, -1, -1  115,042,024   52.43%   Acceptable  Object is not seen yet.
      1, 0, 3, 0        3,892   <0.01%  Interesting  Seeing partially constructed object.
      1, 0, 3, 4       14,291   <0.01%  Interesting  Seeing partially constructed object.
      1, 2, 3, 0          123   <0.01%  Interesting  Seeing partially constructed object.
      1, 2, 3, 4  104,365,974   47.56%   Acceptable  Seen the complete object.

About 18,000 of 219 million readers found blank pages. That's rare, but a busy shop takes a lot of card payments. On an AArch64 machine, a 64-bit ARM one, the same sample saw almost every mix of zeros and real values.

You may wonder how the x86 machine did it, when Why your loop never stops showed that x86 keeps its stores in order. The sample checks that too. When it asks the JIT to keep those accesses in order, the half-built objects vanish on x86_64 and stay on ARM. On x86, the JIT moved the stores.

Publishing through a plain field fails in a second way you met in Why your loop never stops: a reader that loops, waiting for the first card, may read the field once and never again. The lab's RateCardRegistry has exactly that bug.

A reader can see a reference before the fields behind it. Never publish through a plain field.

So the envelope can arrive with blank pages, or not at all. Next, we'll seal it, so the reference and the fields arrive together.

sections.h: Sealing the envelope: four safe ways to publish
sections.html:
An object is safely published when the reference and the state the object had at that moment reach the reader together. In the letter's terms, the envelope is sealed: whoever opens it finds every page that was inside when you sealed it. Java Concurrency in Practice, the classic book on the subject, lists four seals:

  1. Build the object in a static initializer, the code that runs once when a class is first used. The JVM runs it under a lock, and every thread that uses the class afterwards sees the result.
  2. Store it in a volatile field or an AtomicReference (the holder for one reference from Atomics and compare-and-set).
  3. Store it in a final field of an object that is itself properly built (the next section).
  4. Store it in a field guarded by a lock, or hand it over through a java.util.concurrent class, such as a concurrent map or queue.

Each seal is an edge you have met before. Seal 1 uses the lock the JVM holds while it initializes a class. Seal 2 is a volatile write and a later read of the same field. Seal 4 is a lock released by one thread and taken by another, or a hand-over through a concurrent collection. Seal 3 is new, and it gets the next section. Everything the loader wrote before the seal reaches a reader who breaks the same seal. Here is the registry with three of them:

Java
// Fixed: three safe ways to publish, in one class
class RateCardRegistry {
    static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard("EUR", Map.of("VISA", 120L));            // 1. static initializer
    private volatile RateCard current = DEFAULT;                                         // 2. volatile field
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, RateCard> byCurrency = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 4. concurrent map

    void publish(RateCard card) {
        current = card;                              // a volatile write seals it
        byCurrency.put(card.currency(), card);       // and so does put
    }

    RateCard current() {
        return current;                              // a volatile read breaks the same seal
    }
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: three safe ways to publish, in one class
class RateCardRegistry {
    companion object {
        val DEFAULT = RateCard("EUR", mapOf("VISA" to 120L))           // 1. static initializer (companion object)
    }
    @Volatile private var current: RateCard = DEFAULT                   // 2. @Volatile property
    private val byCurrency = ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateCard>()     // 4. concurrent map

    fun publish(card: RateCard) {
        current = card                               // a volatile write seals it
        byCurrency[card.currency] = card             // and so does put
    }

    fun current(): RateCard = current                // a volatile read breaks the same seal
}

Both versions do the same three things. Kotlin's companion object is initialized together with its class, just like a Java static initializer, so seal 1 works the same way, and @Volatile is Kotlin's volatile.

Notice that both sides take part. The loader writes the volatile field, and the reader reads that same field. A seal only the writer uses is no seal. A synchronized publish method with a plain getter, for example, gives the reader no edge at all, because the reader never takes the lock.

Which seal should you pick? For something you replace while the program runs, such as the current rate card, use a volatile field or an AtomicReference. For a constant, use static final. Don't add synchronized getters only to publish: a volatile read costs less and says what you mean.

Hand an object to another thread through a seal: a volatile field, a static initializer, a lock or a concurrent collection.

A seal covers the pages that were inside when you sealed the envelope. If the loader changes the rate card after publishing it, each change needs a seal of its own. That's why the easiest objects to publish are the ones that never change, and Java keeps a special promise for them.

try.title: Sealed or not?
steps: For each line, decide whether a request thread is guaranteed to see the whole RateCard. Name the seal, or the missing edge.
(a) static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...), read by any thread.
(b) private RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads.
(c) private volatile RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads.
(d) cards.put(id, card) on a ConcurrentHashMap, and request threads call cards.get(id).
try.expect: (a) Sealed: the static initializer runs under the JVM's class-initialization lock. (b) Not sealed: there's no edge, so a reader may see a half-built card, or never see it at all. (c) Sealed: a volatile write, then a volatile read of the same field. (d) Sealed: putting a card into a concurrent map happens-before a get that returns it.

sections.h: Final fields arrive whole, even without a seal
sections.html:
final fields get one extra promise from the Java memory model, the rules for what one thread sees of another thread's writes. The Java Language Specification (section 17.5) says, in plain words: a thread that sees a reference to an object only after the object's constructor has finished is guaranteed to see the correct values of its final fields. No volatile and no lock are needed. The promise holds even when the reference reached the reader through a data race, a write and a read of the same field with no edge between them.

The promise reaches through the field. If a final field points to a map or an array, the reader also sees its contents as they were when the constructor ended. The specification calls the end of the constructor the freeze: that's when the final fields are frozen.

In the letter's terms, final fields are pages glued into the envelope at the factory. However the envelope travels, sealed or not, whoever opens it finds those pages in place.

Here's a fee quote with both kinds of field:

Java
final class Quote {
    private final String scheme;            // final: correct even through a race
    private final Map<String, Long> fees;   // final: and the map's contents as of the freeze
    private long hits;                      // plain: a racing reader may see 0

    Quote(String scheme, Map<String, Long> fees) {
        this.scheme = scheme;
        this.fees = Map.copyOf(fees);
    }
}
Kotlin
class Quote(scheme: String, fees: Map<String, Long>) {
    private val scheme = scheme                 // val: a final field, correct even through a race
    private val fees = fees.toMap()             // val: and the map's contents as of the freeze
    private var hits = 0L                       // var: a plain field, a racing reader may see 0
}

The Kotlin version is the same class: a val compiles to a final field, and a var to a plain one. The Try it below checks that in the compiled classes.

Back to BasicJMM_08_Finals. Its last test makes all four fields final and publishes the object through the same plain field. The recorded results, on x86_64 and on AArch64 alike, show readers seeing either no object or the complete one: not one partial object. The test now marks every other result as forbidden.

How does the JVM keep this promise? When a constructor writes a final field, HotSpot, the JVM most people run, puts a barrier at the end of the constructor. Every store before the barrier must be visible before any store after it, and the store that publishes the reference always comes after. On x86 the barrier costs nothing, because the processor keeps stores in order anyway; it only stops the JIT from moving stores past it. On ARM it's a real fence instruction, one that makes the processor finish the earlier stores first.

Put the pieces together and you get the immutable object from Don't share: a final class, every field final, changing inputs copied in the constructor, nothing changeable handed out, and no this handed to anyone before the constructor ends. Don't share showed that such an object needs no lock. Here is the reason underneath: thanks to the final-field promise, no reader can see it half-built, however it arrived. Records and Kotlin classes with only val properties get you most of the way. They still keep a caller's list as it is, so copy it, for example in a record's compact constructor, the one with no parameter list: record FeeSchedule(List<Fee> fees) { FeeSchedule { fees = List.copyOf(fees); } }.

The promise has two limits. Final fields don't deliver the envelope: a reader that waits on a plain field may still never see the reference at all. That's why the lab's RateCardRegistry needs volatile even after RateCard becomes immutable. And the promise starts at the freeze, so it only holds if nobody got the reference before the constructor finished.

Final fields arrive whole through any race, but they don't deliver the reference. Make the data final, and still publish it through a seal.

That second limit is easy to break without noticing. Next, we'll see how a constructor hands out its object too early.

try.title: Find final in the compiled classes
steps: Run both demos below once (the Java one, then the Kotlin one), so Gradle compiles them.
javap is a JDK tool that prints what's inside a compiled class. Predict first: which fields will say final?
From labs/, run javap -p 'jmm/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo$Quote.class', then the same for FinalFieldsDemo$MutableQuote.class.

code.title: FinalFieldsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l04; /** Where final fields come from in Java. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ public class FinalFieldsDemo { // a record's components become private final fields record Quote(String scheme, long feeCents) {} // for contrast: plain, non-final fields static final class MutableQuote { String scheme; long feeCents; } public static void main(String[] args) { Quote q = new Quote("VISA", 120); MutableQuote m = new MutableQuote(); m.scheme = "MC"; m.feeCents = 135; System.out.println(q + " and a mutable quote for " + m.scheme); } }

alt.title: FinalFieldsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l04 /** Where final fields come from in Kotlin. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ class KQuote(val scheme: String, val feeCents: Long) // val: a private final backing field class KMutableQuote(var scheme: String, var feeCents: Long) // var: a private, non-final backing field fun main() { val q = KQuote("VISA", 120) val m = KMutableQuote("MC", 135) m.feeCents = 140 println("${q.scheme} ${q.feeCents} and a mutable quote for ${m.scheme} ${m.feeCents}") }

try.expect: The record and KQuote both show private final java.lang.String scheme; and private final long feeCents;. MutableQuote and KMutableQuote show the same fields without final, and the Kotlin one also has setters. A Kotlin val and a Java record component compile to the same thing, a final field, and they get the final-field promise with it.

sections.h: Don't open the house early: keeping this inside the constructor
sections.html:
Picture a new house and the agent who will sell it. The builders work first: walls, floor, wiring. When they're done, the agent hands out the address and opens the door to buyers. Now picture an agent who hands out the address on the first morning. A buyer arrives while the floor is still a hole in the ground.

A constructor is the builders' work, and this, the reference to the object being built, is the address. Handing this to other code before the constructor ends is called escaping this. The code that receives it is the early buyer: it sees the object with some fields still at their defaults. It doesn't even need another thread.

this escapes when a constructor:

  • registers the object as a listener (an object that other code calls when something happens);
  • starts a thread, or hands over a task, that uses the object;
  • creates a lambda or inner class that captures this and hands it out;
  • calls a method that a subclass can override.

Here's the first case. An event bus is a notice board inside a program: code pins up events, and every registered listener hears each one. The lab's EventBus also replays its last event to each new listener the moment it registers. This listener texts the shop manager about any sale over a limit:

Java
// Naive: `this` escapes before the fields are set
class BigSaleAlert implements Consumer<SaleEvent> {
    private final long limitCents;
    private final Phone manager;

    BigSaleAlert(EventBus bus, long limitCents, Phone manager) {
        bus.register(this);                    // the bus calls accept() right here...
        this.limitCents = limitCents;          // ...before these fields are set
        this.manager = manager;
    }

    public void accept(SaleEvent e) {
        if (e.amountCents() > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: " + e);   // manager is still null
    }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: `this` escapes before the properties are set
class BigSaleAlert(bus: EventBus, limitCents: Long, manager: Phone) : Consumer<SaleEvent> {
    init {
        bus.register(this)                     // the bus calls accept() right here...
    }
    private val limitCents = limitCents        // ...before these properties are set
    private val manager = manager

    override fun accept(e: SaleEvent) {
        if (e.amountCents > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: $e")   // manager is still null
    }
}

register calls accept at once, to replay the last sale. At that moment limitCents is still 0, so every sale looks big, and manager is still null, so manager.text throws a NullPointerException. No second thread was involved. The buyer came in through a call the constructor made itself.

Kotlin runs init blocks and property initializers in the order you write them, so the same bug is one misplaced init away. Kotlin's null safety doesn't save you either: manager is declared non-null, and in the early call it still reads as null. The thread case is in the Try it: a constructor starts a heartbeat thread, which sends a regular "still running" message, and only then looks up the address to send it to. The heartbeat thread is punctual. It reports for work 50 ms before its address exists.

The picture breaks here: on a building site, someone would see the buyer and stop them. In Java, nothing does. The early call looks like any other call.

You might move register to the last line of the constructor. In this one-thread case it works, but it's still the wrong fix. The final-field promise starts when the constructor returns, so threads that get the object from the bus get no promise at all. And if someone writes a subclass, its constructor runs after yours, while the bus already holds the object. Instead, keep constructors to setting fields, and wire the object up once it's built, in a static factory method or a start() method:

Java
// Fixed: the constructor only sets fields; a factory wires it up
// (the fields and accept() stay as they were)
private BigSaleAlert(long limitCents, Phone manager) {
    this.limitCents = limitCents;
    this.manager = manager;
}

static BigSaleAlert listenOn(EventBus bus, long limitCents, Phone manager) {
    BigSaleAlert alert = new BigSaleAlert(limitCents, manager);   // 1. finish building
    bus.register(alert);                                          // 2. then show it to others
    return alert;
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: the constructor only sets properties; a factory wires it up
class BigSaleAlert private constructor(
    private val limitCents: Long,
    private val manager: Phone,
) : Consumer<SaleEvent> {

    override fun accept(e: SaleEvent) {
        if (e.amountCents > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: $e")
    }

    companion object {
        fun listenOn(bus: EventBus, limitCents: Long, manager: Phone): BigSaleAlert {
            val alert = BigSaleAlert(limitCents, manager)   // 1. finish building
            bus.register(alert)                             // 2. then show it to others
            return alert
        }
    }
}

A constructor sets fields and nothing else. Wire the object up after it's built.

Every tool in this lesson hands over an object that is already built. None of them helps when several threads ask for an object that doesn't exist yet, and the first one to ask has to build it while the others wait. That's the next lesson's problem.

try.title: A thread that starts too early
steps: Read ThisEscapeDemo. Its constructor starts a heartbeat thread, then looks up the address to send to, which takes about 50 ms.
Predict both lines of output, then run it.
Fix it: move the thread start out of the constructor into a start() method, and call start() from main after construction. Run it again.

code.title: ThisEscapeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l04; /** * A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its fields. * A heartbeat is a short "still running" message that one program sends another every few seconds. */ public class ThisEscapeDemo { static final class HeartbeatSender { private final String endpoint; HeartbeatSender(String endpointName) { Thread beat = new Thread(this::sendHeartbeat, "heartbeat"); beat.start(); // `this` escapes to another thread here... this.endpoint = resolve(endpointName); // ...and this final field is set about 50 ms later } void sendHeartbeat() { System.out.println("heartbeat thread sends to: " + endpoint); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { HeartbeatSender sender = new HeartbeatSender("head-office"); System.out.println("constructor finished, endpoint = " + sender.endpoint); Thread.sleep(100); } // stands in for a slow lookup of the address over the network static String resolve(String name) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "https://" + name + ".example.com"; } }

alt.title: ThisEscapeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** * A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its properties. * A heartbeat is a short "still running" message that one program sends another every few seconds. */ private class HeartbeatClient(endpointName: String) { val endpoint: String init { thread(name = "heartbeat") { sendHeartbeat() } // `this` escapes to another thread here... endpoint = resolve(endpointName) // ...and this val is set about 50 ms later } fun sendHeartbeat() { println("heartbeat thread sends to: $endpoint") // a non-null String that reads as null } } fun main() { val sender = HeartbeatClient("head-office") println("constructor finished, endpoint = ${sender.endpoint}") Thread.sleep(100) } // stands in for a slow lookup of the address over the network private fun resolve(name: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) return "https://$name.example.com" }

try.expect: The first run prints heartbeat thread sends to: null, then constructor finished, endpoint = https://head-office.example.com. The heartbeat thread ran while the constructor was still looking up the address. In Kotlin, val endpoint: String is non-null by its type and still reads as null. After the fix, the heartbeat prints the real address: the field was set before start(), and start() happens-before everything the new thread does.

aside.title: What if a framework builds my objects?
aside.html: If you write web services, a framework often creates your objects for you and passes in what they need. Most frameworks can also call a setup method once the object is fully built. In Spring and in Jakarta EE, two widely used Java frameworks for web services, that's a method marked @PostConstruct. Put listener registration, timers and threads there, not in the constructor. The rule is the same; the framework just gives the after-it's-built step a name.

compare.title: An immutable rate card in Java and Kotlin

java.title: RateCard.java
java.html: public final class RateCard { private final String currency; private final Map<String, Long> feesByScheme; public RateCard(String currency, Map<String, Long> feesByScheme) { this.currency = currency; this.feesByScheme = Map.copyOf(feesByScheme); // our own unmodifiable copy } public String currency() { return currency; } public Map<String, Long> feesByScheme() { return feesByScheme; } // safe to hand out }

kotlin.title: RateCard.kt
kotlin.html: class RateCard(val currency: String, feesByScheme: Map<String, Long>) { // our own copy, behind a read-only type val feesByScheme: Map<String, Long> = feesByScheme.toMap() }

compare.note: Both classes have final fields and copy the caller's map, so both get the final-field promise. Kotlin says it in three lines, because Kotlin classes are final by default and a val compiles to a private final field with a getter. The real difference is the map. Java's Map.copyOf returns a map that nobody can change. Kotlin's Map is a read-only interface: toMap() gives you a private LinkedHashMap, and code that casts it to MutableMap could still change it. Inside your own code that's usually fine. If the object travels to code you don't control, build the copy with java.util.Map.copyOf instead, as Don't share did.

worked.title: Publish the shop's delivery settings safely

steps.say: The shop charges a delivery fee, and delivery is free for orders above a threshold. A helper thread fetches new settings from head office every minute, and every till thread reads them. Now and then a till charges the new fee with the old threshold, a pair head office never set. Find both problems.
steps.code: public class DeliverySettingsHolder { private DeliverySettings settings = new DeliverySettings(); // 1. a changeable object in a plain field void refresh(HeadOffice office) { // the helper thread, every minute Settings s = office.fetch(); settings.setFeeCents(s.feeCents()); // 2. changed in place... settings.setFreeAboveCents(s.freeAboveCents()); // ...one field at a time } public DeliverySettings current() { return settings; } // 3. every till reads it }

alt.html: class DeliverySettingsHolder { private var settings = DeliverySettings() // 1. a changeable object in a plain property fun refresh(office: HeadOffice) { // the helper thread, every minute val s = office.fetch() settings.feeCents = s.feeCents // 2. changed in place... settings.freeAboveCents = s.freeAboveCents // ...one field at a time } fun current(): DeliverySettings = settings // 3. every till reads it }

steps.say: First, the helper changes one shared object in place, field by field, with no lock. A till can read between the two writes and get the new fee next to the old threshold. Second, nothing publishes the settings safely. Their fields are plain, and there's no edge from the helper thread to the tills, so a till may see the writes late or in any order. Even a lock around refresh wouldn't help tills that never take it.
Make the settings immutable, build a whole new object on each refresh, and publish it with one volatile write. Each till then gets one complete version.
steps.code: public record DeliverySettings(long feeCents, long freeAboveCents) {} // 1. immutable: final fields, no setters public class DeliverySettingsHolder { private volatile DeliverySettings settings = new DeliverySettings(499, 5_000); void refresh(HeadOffice office) { Settings s = office.fetch(); settings = new DeliverySettings(s.feeCents(), s.freeAboveCents()); // 2. build a new one, 3. publish it } public DeliverySettings current() { return settings; } // 4. one complete version per read }

alt.html: data class DeliverySettings(val feeCents: Long, val freeAboveCents: Long) // 1. immutable: vals only class DeliverySettingsHolder { @Volatile private var settings = DeliverySettings(499, 5_000) fun refresh(office: HeadOffice) { val s = office.fetch() settings = DeliverySettings(s.feeCents, s.freeAboveCents) // 2. build a new one, 3. publish it } fun current(): DeliverySettings = settings // 4. one complete version per read }

steps.say: Why both changes? The record alone makes each version safe to read through any race, thanks to its final fields, but a till might keep reading an old reference for a long time. The volatile field alone delivers the reference, but a changeable object behind it could still change under a till. An immutable object behind a volatile reference fixes both. One habit completes it: a till calls current() once per sale and keeps that version for the whole sale.

lab.title: Fix an escaping constructor and an unsafe publication
steps: Meet the classes. RateCard holds the card fees for one currency. RateCardRegistry holds the current rate card: a loader thread calls publish, and request threads call current() or wait for the first card in awaitFirst(). FraudMonitor listens on an EventBus and flags any payment over a limit. The bus and PaymentEvent are given and need no changes.
Run the tests once. All six fail. The two FraudMonitor tests fail with a NullPointerException thrown from inside the constructor.
Make RateCard immutable: a final class, final fields, and Map.copyOf in the constructor. Keep the public constructor and methods.
Publish safely in RateCardRegistry. Then ask yourself: once RateCard is immutable, why does the waiting reader still need this change?
Fix FraudMonitor so the bus can't see the monitor before its constructor has finished. create stays the only way to make one.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Map.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy, so feesByScheme() can return the field as it is.
Final fields make a RateCard safe to read once a thread has the reference. They do nothing to deliver the reference to a thread that loops on a plain field.
In FraudMonitor, the private constructor should only set fields. Build the monitor in create, then register it, then return it.
lab.done: All six tests in SafePublicationTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: An immutable fee schedule from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write FeeSchedule with a currency and a list of fees, immutable and safe to share through any race. Then write a holder that publishes the latest schedule to request threads. Check: what would break if you skipped the copy?

answer.html: public final class FeeSchedule { // final: no changeable subclasses private final String currency; // final fields: safe through a race private final List<Fee> fees; public FeeSchedule(String currency, List<Fee> fees) { this.currency = currency; this.fees = List.copyOf(fees); // copy in: the caller can't change ours } public String currency() { return currency; } public List<Fee> fees() { return fees; } // unmodifiable: safe to hand out } public final class FeeScheduleHolder { private volatile FeeSchedule current; // volatile: each new schedule is published safely public void replace(FeeSchedule next) { current = next; } public FeeSchedule current() { return current; } } // Without the copy, the caller still holds the list and can change it under every reader.

alt.html: class FeeSchedule(val currency: String, fees: List<Fee>) { // final by default val fees: List<Fee> = java.util.List.copyOf(fees) // copy in: the caller can't change ours } class FeeScheduleHolder { @Volatile var current: FeeSchedule? = null // each new schedule is published safely private set fun replace(next: FeeSchedule) { current = next } } // Without the copy, the caller still holds the list and can change it under every reader.

recap: Publishing an object means storing a reference to it where another thread can find it. Through a plain field, a reader can see the reference before the constructor's writes, or never see it at all.

Safe publication seals the envelope: a static initializer, a volatile field or AtomicReference, a final field of a properly built object, or a lock or java.util.concurrent hand-over. The writer and the reader must use the same seal.
Final fields are seen as the constructor left them, even through a data race. They don't make the reference itself visible.

An immutable object (final class, final fields, copied inputs, nothing changeable handed out, no escaping this) is safe to share however it's published. For data you replace, publish a new immutable object with one volatile write.
this escapes when a constructor registers it, starts a thread with it, or hands out a lambda that captures it. Set fields in the constructor, and wire the object up afterwards.
The limit: these tools hand over an object that's already built. Building it on first use, while other threads ask for it too, needs more.

explain.prompt: FraudMonitor had only final fields, yet the bus's replayed event hit a NullPointerException inside it. Explain why in your own words, and why moving register to the end of the constructor is not the right fix.
explain.answer: The constructor handed this to the bus before it set its fields, and the bus called accept straight away to replay its last event. At that moment flagged and limitCents still held their default values, null and 0, so flagged.add threw. Final fields don't help, because their promise starts when the constructor returns, and the object was used before that. Moving register to the last line would make this one-thread case work. But threads that get the monitor from the bus would still get it before its constructor finished, with no final-field promise, and a subclass constructor would run even later. The right fix is to only set fields in the constructor and register the finished object from a factory method.

deeper.html:
The final-field promise has a few edges worth knowing.

It covers what the constructor set, and what the final fields point to, as of the freeze. If you change an object that a final field points to after the constructor, those later changes get no promise. That's why "effectively immutable" objects, objects nobody changes after publishing although nothing stops them, still need a seal, while truly immutable objects don't.

Reflection can break final. Reflection is the part of Java that lets code look at and change classes and fields while the program runs. Some frameworks have long used it to write final fields after construction (Field.setAccessible(true), then set), and the memory model gives such writes almost no guarantees. JDK 26 starts closing that door with JEP 500, "Prepare to Make Final Mean Final". By default it prints a warning when reflection changes a final field, and a later release is planned to make that an error unless you allow it. Libraries that turn objects into bytes and back, and tools that build fake objects for tests, are the usual sources of these warnings.

The static-initializer seal works because class initialization is itself a careful hand-over. The JVM initializes each class once, under a lock, and any thread that then uses the class is guaranteed to see what the static initializer wrote. The next lesson builds lazy initialization on exactly that.

Aleksey Shipilëv's "Safe Publication and Safe Initialization in Java" separates the two ideas this lesson combines: safe publication (the seal) and safe initialization (final fields). It also measures what each one costs.
